what_it_does: This paper addresses a massive scalability challenge in brain-computer interfaces that aim to record from a million electrodes simultaneously. Two constraints make this hard: first, the ADCs that digitize each electrode's signal consume too much power—over 50 times the efficiency target of 10 nanowatts per input; second, reading from a million electrodes at high sampling rate produces 200 gigabits per second of data, too much to transmit. The solution exploits a natural property of neural spiking: neurons only fire intermittently, so most recorded channels carry silence most of the time. The design uses event-driven logic that only captures and transmits when interesting activity occurs (spatially selective zooming), a very efficient ADC fabric built from reconfigurable inverters operating at the 10-nanowatt target, and adaptive bit-width quantization that uses fewer bits for quieter channels and more for active ones.
